title: Wordless soprano
summary: Soaring wordless soprano built on formants. The line that turns a western cue into ecstasy; nothing goes above it.
notes:
The soaring wordless soprano over the whole orchestra — Edda Dell'Orso's line, the thing that turns a western cue into the ecstasy of gold. A `lead`, because it is the top line and nothing else in the arrangement is allowed above it. **No amp**, obviously.

**A sung vowel is three formants, and everything else is decoration.** `body` is that vowel: 800 Hz and 1180 Hz are F1 and F2 of an open "ah", 2900 Hz is the singer's formant — the narrow resonance a trained voice develops so it can be heard over an orchestra without a microphone — and the −4 dB at 350 Hz thins the chest, because this is a soprano at the top of her range rather than a mezzo. Those frequencies are absolute and stay put while the note moves, which is the whole reason the block exists: a voice sings *the same vowel* at every pitch, so the harmonics slide underneath fixed resonances and the timbre changes across the register. A synth patch transposes instead, and that is why every synth choir sounds identical at every note.

**The vibrato is the tell, so it is large.** 5.8 Hz at 0.055 — wider than the violin's 0.045 and far wider than the whistle's — because an operatic soprano's vibrato is not an ornament she adds, it is how the voice is produced at that pressure. Drift is 0.35: enough that it is never mechanical, but less than a whistler's, since a trained voice is a *controlled* instability.

The envelope is slower than any other lead here: 120 ms attack, 0.9 sustain, 0.5 s release. A voice has to be supported before it speaks, and the half-second tail is the singer releasing the note rather than the room — anything longer starts sounding like reverb printed into the instrument, which makes it impossible to place in a mix later.

The filter envelope opens (0.15 s to a 0.75 sustain, 3.6 octaves off 300 Hz) rather than collapsing, for the same reason as the bow: pressure builds after the note starts. Q is 0.5 — the brightness of this voice is meant to come from the singer's formant in `body`, and a resonant filter on top of a resonant body is where a vocal patch starts to whistle at you.

`breath` is deliberately the quietest of the wind voices at 0.035, with a slow 60 ms follower. A trained singer wastes very little air, so the noise is a swell under the note rather than a consonant at the front of it. It is still not zero, and taking it to zero is what makes the difference between a soprano and a theremin.
